back.text: Cleopatra VII — Last active pharaoh of Ptolemaic Egypt (69–30 BCE). She defended her dynasty through alliances with Julius Caesar and Mark Antony; her death preceded Rome's annexation of Egypt.
back.markdown:
**Last active pharaoh of Ptolemaic Egypt (69–30 BCE).**

{#0F766E}Why they matter{/}

- She defended her dynasty through alliances with Julius Caesar and Mark Antony.
- Her death preceded Rome's annexation of Egypt.

back.text: Julius Caesar — Roman general and statesman (100–44 BCE). He conquered Gaul, crossed the Rubicon, became dictator, and helped end the Roman Republic before his assassination.
back.markdown:
**Roman general and statesman (100–44 BCE).**

{#0F766E}Why they matter{/}

- He conquered Gaul and crossed the Rubicon.
- He became dictator and helped end the Roman Republic before his assassination.

back.text: Augustus — Rome's first emperor (63 BCE–14 CE). He defeated Antony and Cleopatra, stabilized Roman rule, and began the long peace called the Pax Romana.
back.markdown:
**Rome's first emperor (63 BCE–14 CE).**

{#0F766E}Why they matter{/}

- He defeated Antony and Cleopatra and became Rome's first emperor.
- He stabilized Roman rule and began the long peace called the Pax Romana.

back.text: Hatshepsut — Female pharaoh of Egypt's 18th Dynasty (c. 1507–1458 BCE). Her reign emphasized trade and monumental building, including her temple at Deir el-Bahri.
Ashoka — Mauryan emperor of India (ruled c. 268–232 BCE). After the Kalinga War he promoted Buddhism, ethical government, and public welfare through inscriptions on rocks and pillars.
back.markdown:
**Mauryan emperor of India (ruled c. 268–232 BCE).**

{#0F766E}Why they matter{/}

- After the Kalinga War, he promoted Buddhism and ethical government.
- His rock and pillar inscriptions encouraged public welfare across the Mauryan Empire.

back.text: Qin Shi Huang — First emperor of a unified China (259–210 BCE). He standardized writing, currency, and measurements; his vast tomb is guarded by the Terracotta Army.
back.markdown:
**First emperor of a unified China (259–210 BCE).**

{#0F766E}Why they matter{/}

- He standardized writing, currency, and measurements across unified China.
- His vast tomb is guarded by the Terracotta Army.

back.text: Emperor Wu of Han — Chinese emperor (156–87 BCE) who greatly expanded Han power and encouraged routes later called the Silk Road. He made Confucian learning central to government.
Wu Zetian — China's only woman to rule as emperor in her own name (624–705). She expanded the civil service examinations and governed during a period of Tang-era strength.
Empress Theodora — Byzantine empress (c. 497–548) and influential partner of Justinian I. She backed legal protections for women and helped steady the government during the Nika riots.
Genghis Khan — Founder of the Mongol Empire (c. 1162–1227). He united Mongol tribes and built a disciplined conquest state that became the basis of history's largest contiguous land empire.
Mansa Musa — Ruler of the Mali Empire (c. 1280–c. 1337), renowned for wealth, a spectacular pilgrimage to Mecca, and patronage that strengthened Timbuktu as a centre of learning.
Mehmed II — Ottoman sultan (1432–1481) known as “the Conqueror.” He captured Constantinople in 1453, ending the Byzantine Empire and making the city an Ottoman capital.
Suleiman the Magnificent — Ottoman sultan (1494–1566) whose empire reached a political and cultural high point. He expanded its territory and codified laws, earning the Turkish title “the Lawgiver.”
Akbar — Mughal emperor of India (1542–1605). He expanded the empire, improved administration, welcomed religious debate, and included diverse elites in government.
back.markdown:
**Mughal emperor of India (1542–1605).**

{#0F766E}Why they matter{/}

- He expanded the Mughal Empire and improved its administration.
- He welcomed religious debate and included diverse elites in government.

back.text: Tokugawa Ieyasu — Japanese warlord (1543–1616) who won at Sekigahara and founded the Tokugawa shogunate. Its rule brought more than two centuries of internal peace.
Elizabeth I — Queen of England and Ireland (1533–1603). Her reign saw the defeat of the Spanish Armada, religious consolidation, maritime expansion, and a flourishing of English drama.
back.markdown:
**Queen of England and Ireland (1533–1603).**

{#0F766E}Why they matter{/}

- Her reign saw the defeat of the Spanish Armada and greater maritime expansion.
- English drama flourished during her rule.

back.text: Napoleon Bonaparte — French general and emperor (1769–1821). He reshaped Europe through war and spread the Napoleonic Code, but was finally defeated at Waterloo.
back.markdown:
**French general and emperor (1769–1821).**

{#0F766E}Why they matter{/}

- He reshaped Europe through a series of wars.
- The Napoleonic Code influenced legal systems far beyond France.
- He was finally defeated at Waterloo.

back.text: Queen Victoria — British monarch (1819–1901) whose 63-year reign gave its name to the Victorian era. Britain industrialized and its empire expanded enormously during her rule.
Shaka Zulu — Zulu king (c. 1787–1828) who built a powerful state in southern Africa through military and political reorganization. Accounts of him mix evidence with later legend.
Menelik II — Emperor of Ethiopia (1844–1913). He expanded and modernized the state, and Ethiopian forces defeated an Italian invasion at Adwa in 1896.
Mustafa Kemal Atatürk — Founder and first president of the Republic of Turkey (1881–1938). He led the independence struggle and introduced sweeping secular and institutional reforms.
back.markdown:
**Founder and first president of the Republic of Turkey (1881–1938).**

{#0F766E}Why they matter{/}

- He led the struggle that established the Republic of Turkey.
- As its first president, he introduced sweeping secular and institutional reforms.

back.text: Isaac Newton — English mathematician and physicist (1642–1727). He formulated laws of motion and universal gravitation, helped develop calculus, and transformed the study of light.
back.markdown:
**English mathematician and physicist (1642–1727).**

{#0F766E}Why they matter{/}

- He formulated the laws of motion and universal gravitation.
- He helped develop calculus and transformed the study of light.

back.text: Galileo Galilei — Italian astronomer and physicist (1564–1642). Telescopic observations supported heliocentrism; his work on motion helped establish experimental science.
back.markdown:
**Italian astronomer and physicist (1564–1642).**

{#0F766E}Why they matter{/}

- His telescopic observations supported heliocentrism.
- His work on motion helped establish experimental science.

back.text: Nicolaus Copernicus — Polish astronomer (1473–1543) who proposed a mathematical model placing the Sun, rather than Earth, near the centre of the planetary system.
Ibn al-Haytham — Arab scholar (c. 965–c. 1040), also called Alhazen. His experiments on light and vision established that sight occurs when light enters the eye.
Ibn Sina — Persian physician and philosopher (c. 980–1037). His Canon of Medicine organized medical knowledge and remained influential for centuries across Eurasia.
Al-Khwarizmi — Persian mathematician (c. 780–c. 850) whose work systematized algebra. The words “algorithm” and, through his book title, “algebra” are linked to him.
Zhang Heng — Han Chinese polymath (78–139). He advanced astronomy and mathematics and devised an early seismoscope that indicated the direction of distant earthquakes.
Charles Darwin — English naturalist (1809–1882) who explained evolution through natural selection. Observations from the HMS Beagle voyage helped shape On the Origin of Species.
back.markdown:
**English naturalist (1809–1882) who explained evolution through natural selection.**

{#0F766E}Why they matter{/}

- He explained evolution through natural selection.
- Observations from the HMS Beagle voyage helped shape On the Origin of Species.

back.text: Louis Pasteur — French chemist and microbiologist (1822–1895). He strengthened germ theory, developed vaccines, and created pasteurization to reduce harmful microbes in food and drink.
back.markdown:
**French chemist and microbiologist (1822–1895).**

{#0F766E}Why they matter{/}

- He strengthened germ theory and developed vaccines.
- Pasteurization uses controlled heating to reduce harmful microbes in food and drink.

back.text: Marie Curie — Polish-born French physicist and chemist (1867–1934). She pioneered radioactivity research, discovered polonium and radium, and became the first person to win two Nobel Prizes.
back.markdown:
**Polish-born French physicist and chemist (1867–1934).**

{#0F766E}Why they matter{/}

- She pioneered research on radioactivity and discovered polonium and radium.
- She became the first person to win two Nobel Prizes.

back.text: Nikola Tesla — Serbian-American inventor (1856–1943) central to practical alternating-current power systems. His work included induction motors, transformers, and high-frequency electrical experiments.
Ada Lovelace — British mathematician (1815–1852). Her notes on Babbage's Analytical Engine included an algorithm, often described as the first published computer program.
Alan Turing — British mathematician (1912–1954). He founded key ideas in computer science and helped break German Enigma-related codes at Bletchley Park during World War II.
back.markdown:
**British mathematician (1912–1954).**

{#0F766E}Why they matter{/}

- He established key foundations of computer science.
- During World War II, he helped break German Enigma-related codes at Bletchley Park.

back.text: Chien-Shiung Wu — Chinese-American experimental physicist (1912–1997). Her 1956 experiment showed that parity symmetry is violated in weak nuclear interactions.
Katherine Johnson — American mathematician (1918–2020) whose orbital calculations supported early NASA crewed missions, including John Glenn's flight and Apollo lunar missions.
Tu Youyou — Chinese pharmaceutical chemist (born 1930) who drew on traditional texts to help discover artemisinin, a highly effective treatment for malaria.
Leonardo da Vinci — Italian Renaissance artist and thinker (1452–1519). He painted the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper and filled notebooks with anatomical and engineering studies.
back.markdown:
**Italian Renaissance artist and thinker (1452–1519).**

{#0F766E}Why they matter{/}

- He painted the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper.
- His notebooks contain influential anatomical and engineering studies.

back.text: Michelangelo — Italian Renaissance sculptor, painter, and architect (1475–1564). He created David and the Pietà, painted the Sistine Chapel ceiling, and worked on St Peter's Basilica.
back.markdown:
**Italian Renaissance sculptor, painter, and architect (1475–1564).**

{#0F766E}Why they matter{/}

- He sculpted David and the Pietà.
- He painted the Sistine Chapel ceiling and worked on St Peter's Basilica.

back.text: William Shakespeare — English playwright and poet (1564–1616). Works such as Hamlet, Macbeth, and Romeo and Juliet transformed drama and deeply influenced the English language.
back.markdown:
**English playwright and poet (1564–1616).**

{#0F766E}Why they matter{/}

- Plays such as Hamlet, Macbeth, and Romeo and Juliet transformed drama.
- His writing deeply influenced the English language.

back.text: Murasaki Shikibu — Japanese court writer (c. 973–c. 1014 or 1025), author of The Tale of Genji, often called the world's first novel.
Jane Austen — English novelist (1775–1817). Pride and Prejudice and her other novels use wit and social observation to examine class, money, and marriage.
Leo Tolstoy — Russian writer (1828–1910), author of War and Peace and Anna Karenina. His later Christian pacifism influenced nonviolent reformers.
Rabindranath Tagore — Bengali poet, composer, and educator (1861–1941). He became the first non-European Nobel literature laureate and wrote songs adopted as the anthems of India and Bangladesh.
back.markdown:
**Bengali poet, composer, and educator (1861–1941).**

{#0F766E}Why they matter{/}

- He became the first non-European Nobel laureate in Literature.
- He wrote songs later adopted as the national anthems of India and Bangladesh.

back.text: Vincent van Gogh — Dutch Post-Impressionist painter (1853–1890). His vivid colour and expressive brushwork shaped modern art; The Starry Night is among his best-known works.
Frida Kahlo — Mexican painter (1907–1954) known for psychologically intense self-portraits exploring identity, pain, disability, and Mexican culture.
Chinua Achebe — Nigerian novelist (1930–2013). Things Fall Apart portrayed Igbo society and colonial disruption, reshaping global understanding of modern African literature.
Socrates — Athenian philosopher (c. 470–399 BCE) known through others' writings. His probing question-and-answer method examined ethics and knowledge; Athens condemned him to death.
back.markdown:
**Athenian philosopher (c. 470–399 BCE) known through others' writings.**

{#0F766E}Why they matter{/}

- His probing question-and-answer method examined ethics and knowledge.
- Athens condemned him to death; his ideas survive through the writings of others.

back.text: Aristotle — Greek philosopher and scientist (384–322 BCE). He wrote across logic, ethics, politics, biology, and rhetoric and tutored Alexander the Great.
back.markdown:
**Greek philosopher and scientist (384–322 BCE).**

{#0F766E}Why they matter{/}

- He wrote influential works on logic, ethics, politics, biology, and rhetoric.
- He also tutored Alexander the Great.

back.text: Confucius — Chinese teacher and philosopher (551–479 BCE). He emphasized ethical conduct, education, family duty, and humane government; his ideas shaped East Asian society for centuries.
back.markdown:
**Chinese teacher and philosopher (551–479 BCE).**

{#0F766E}Why they matter{/}

- He emphasized ethical conduct, education, family duty, and humane government.
- His ideas shaped East Asian society for centuries.

back.text: Sun Tzu — Traditionally regarded as an ancient Chinese strategist associated with The Art of War. His exact identity and the text's authorship are debated by historians.
Laozi — Traditionally credited as the ancient Chinese author of the Dao De Jing and a foundational figure in Daoism; historians debate whether he was one person.
Hypatia — Alexandrian philosopher, mathematician, and astronomer (c. 355–415). A prominent teacher in late antiquity, her murder became a symbol of sectarian conflict.
Mary Wollstonecraft — English writer (1759–1797) whose A Vindication of the Rights of Woman argued that women deserve education and rational equality.
Karl Marx — German philosopher and economist (1818–1883). With Friedrich Engels he wrote The Communist Manifesto; his critique of capitalism profoundly influenced politics and social theory.
back.markdown:
**German philosopher and economist (1818–1883).**

{#0F766E}Why they matter{/}

- With Friedrich Engels, he wrote The Communist Manifesto.
- His critique of capitalism profoundly influenced politics and social theory.

back.text: Zheng He — Chinese Muslim admiral (1371–1433) who led seven enormous Ming voyages across the Indian Ocean, reaching Southeast Asia, Arabia, and East Africa.
Ibn Battuta — Moroccan traveller (1304–1368/69) who journeyed across Africa, Eurasia, and the Indian Ocean world, covering more distance than Marco Polo.
Sacagawea — Lemhi Shoshone woman (c. 1788–after 1812) who interpreted and helped guide the Lewis and Clark expedition across western North America.
Ernest Shackleton — Anglo-Irish Antarctic explorer (1874–1922). After Endurance was trapped and crushed by ice, his leadership helped bring every expedition member home alive.
back.markdown:
**Anglo-Irish Antarctic explorer (1874–1922).**

{#0F766E}Why they matter{/}

- He led the Endurance expedition after its ship was trapped and crushed by Antarctic ice.
- His leadership helped bring every expedition member home alive.

back.text: Amelia Earhart — American aviation pioneer (1897–disappeared 1937). She was the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic and vanished during an attempted round-the-world flight.
Yuri Gagarin — Soviet cosmonaut (1934–1968) who became the first human in space, completing one orbit of Earth aboard Vostok 1 in 1961.
Tupaia — Ra'iatean navigator and priest (c. 1725–1770). His Pacific knowledge, translation, and charting were vital during James Cook's first voyage.
Joan of Arc — French heroine (c. 1412–1431) who inspired forces during the Hundred Years' War and helped secure Charles VII's coronation; she was later canonized.
back.markdown:
**French heroine (c. 1412–1431).**

{#0F766E}Why they matter{/}

- She inspired French forces during the Hundred Years' War and helped secure Charles VII's coronation.
- She was later canonized as a saint.

back.text: George Washington — Commander of the American revolutionary army and first US president (1732–1799). He established precedents including voluntarily leaving office after two terms.
back.markdown:
**Commander of the American revolutionary army and first US president (1732–1799).**

{#0F766E}Why they matter{/}

- He commanded the American revolutionary army and became the first US president.
- He set important precedents, including voluntarily leaving office after two terms.

back.text: Toussaint Louverture — Formerly enslaved Haitian revolutionary leader (c. 1743–1803). He helped defeat slavery and foreign armies, laying foundations for Haitian independence.
Simón Bolívar — Venezuelan military and political leader (1783–1830) who helped liberate several South American territories from Spanish rule, earning the title “El Libertador.”
José de San Martín — Argentine general (1778–1850) central to the independence of Argentina, Chile, and Peru. His army famously crossed the Andes in 1817.
Emiliano Zapata — Mexican revolutionary (1879–1919) who demanded land reform under the slogan “Land and Liberty.” His movement represented rural communities in southern Mexico.
Harriet Tubman — American abolitionist (c. 1822–1913) who escaped slavery and repeatedly guided others to freedom through the Underground Railroad; she also served the Union during the Civil War.
back.markdown:
**American abolitionist (c. 1822–1913).**

{#0F766E}Why they matter{/}

- After escaping slavery, she repeatedly guided others to freedom through the Underground Railroad.
- She also served the Union during the American Civil War.

back.text: Frederick Douglass — American abolitionist, writer, and orator (c. 1818–1895). After escaping slavery, his autobiographies and speeches powerfully argued for emancipation and equal rights.
Florence Nightingale — British nursing reformer (1820–1910). During and after the Crimean War she used sanitation, training, and statistics to professionalize nursing and improve hospitals.
back.markdown:
**British nursing reformer (1820–1910).**

{#0F766E}Why they matter{/}

- She used sanitation and statistics to improve military and civilian hospitals.
- Her work helped professionalize nursing and nursing education.

back.text: Emmeline Pankhurst — British suffrage leader (1858–1928) who founded the Women's Social and Political Union, known for militant campaigning for women's voting rights.
Mahatma Gandhi — Indian independence leader (1869–1948) who mobilized mass nonviolent resistance against British rule. His methods influenced civil-rights movements worldwide.
back.markdown:
**Indian independence leader (1869–1948) who mobilized mass nonviolent resistance against British rule.**

{#0F766E}Why they matter{/}

- He mobilized mass nonviolent resistance against British rule in India.
- His methods influenced civil-rights movements around the world.

back.text: Martin Luther King Jr. — American civil-rights leader (1929–1968) who championed nonviolent protest against segregation and racial injustice and delivered the “I Have a Dream” speech.
back.markdown:
**American civil-rights leader (1929–1968).**

{#0F766E}Why they matter{/}

- He championed nonviolent protest against segregation and racial injustice.
- He delivered the landmark “I Have a Dream” speech.

back.text: Nelson Mandela — South African anti-apartheid leader and president (1918–2013). Imprisoned for 27 years, he later helped negotiate democratic rule and promoted reconciliation.
back.markdown:
**South African anti-apartheid leader and president (1918–2013).**

{#0F766E}Why they matter{/}

- He spent 27 years imprisoned for opposing apartheid.
- He later helped negotiate democratic rule and promoted reconciliation as South Africa's president.

back.text: Rosa Parks — American civil-rights activist (1913–2005). Her 1955 refusal to surrender a bus seat helped spark the Montgomery bus boycott; she had long worked with the NAACP.
back.markdown:
**American civil-rights activist (1913–2005).**

{#0F766E}Why they matter{/}

- Her 1955 refusal to surrender a bus seat helped spark the Montgomery bus boycott.
- She had already worked for years with the NAACP.

back.text: Wangari Maathai — Kenyan environmentalist and democracy activist (1940–2011) who founded the Green Belt Movement and became the first African woman awarded the Nobel Peace Prize.
Mozart — Austrian composer (1756–1791) whose operas, symphonies, and concertos combined brilliance and emotional depth. A child prodigy, he composed more than 600 works.
back.markdown:
**Austrian composer (1756–1791) whose operas, symphonies, and concertos combined brilliance and emotional depth.**

{#0F766E}Why they matter{/}

- His operas, symphonies, and concertos combined technical brilliance with emotional depth.
- A child prodigy, he composed more than 600 works.

back.text: Beethoven — German composer (1770–1827) who bridged Classical and Romantic music. He created major works, including the Ninth Symphony, despite severe hearing loss.
back.markdown:
**German composer (1770–1827) who bridged Classical and Romantic music.**

{#0F766E}Why they matter{/}

- He helped bridge the Classical and Romantic eras of music.
- He created major works, including the Ninth Symphony, despite severe hearing loss.

front.markdown: Who became the first non-European Nobel laureate in Literature?

back.text: Rabindranath Tagore — The Bengali poet received the 1913 prize; his writing and songs influenced culture across South Asia.

Nzinga of Ndongo and Matamba — Queen of Ndongo and Matamba in west-central Africa (1583–1663). She resisted Portuguese expansion through warfare, diplomacy, and shifting alliances. Her long reign made her an enduring symbol of Angolan independence and leadership.
back.markdown:
**Queen of Ndongo and Matamba in west-central Africa (1583–1663).**

{#0F766E}Why they matter{/}

- She resisted Portuguese expansion through warfare, diplomacy, and shifting alliances.
- Her long reign made her an enduring symbol of Angolan independence and leadership.

back.text: Yaa Asantewaa — Asante queen mother in present-day Ghana (c. 1840–1921). She led the 1900 resistance known as the War of the Golden Stool against British colonial rule. She became a major symbol of anticolonial courage in Ghana.
back.markdown:
**Asante queen mother in present-day Ghana (c. 1840–1921).**

{#0F766E}Why they matter{/}

- She led the 1900 resistance known as the War of the Golden Stool against British colonial rule.
- She became a major symbol of anticolonial courage in Ghana.

back.text: Haile Selassie — Emperor of Ethiopia (1892–1975). He appealed to the League of Nations after Fascist Italy invaded Ethiopia. He later helped establish the Organization of African Unity in Addis Ababa.
back.markdown:
**Emperor of Ethiopia (1892–1975).**

{#0F766E}Why they matter{/}

- He appealed to the League of Nations after Fascist Italy invaded Ethiopia.
- He later helped establish the Organization of African Unity in Addis Ababa.

back.text: Chandragupta Maurya — Founder of the Mauryan Empire in ancient India (reigned c. 321–297 BCE). He unified much of northern India under a centralized state. The empire he founded later reached its height under his grandson Ashoka.
back.markdown:
**Founder of the Mauryan Empire in ancient India (reigned c. 321–297 BCE).**

{#0F766E}Why they matter{/}

- He unified much of northern India under a centralized state.
- The empire he founded later reached its height under his grandson Ashoka.

back.text: Rani Lakshmibai — Queen of Jhansi and leader in the Indian Rebellion of 1857 (c. 1828–1858). She fought British annexation of her kingdom. Her courage made her an enduring symbol of resistance to colonial rule.
back.markdown:
**Queen of Jhansi and leader in the Indian Rebellion of 1857 (c. 1828–1858).**

{#0F766E}Why they matter{/}

- She fought British annexation of her kingdom.
- Her courage made her an enduring symbol of resistance to colonial rule.

back.text: B. R. Ambedkar — Indian jurist, reformer, and statesman (1891–1956). He chaired the committee that drafted India's Constitution. He campaigned against caste discrimination and for the rights of Dalits.
back.markdown:
**Indian jurist, reformer, and statesman (1891–1956).**

{#0F766E}Why they matter{/}

- He chaired the committee that drafted India's Constitution.
- He campaigned against caste discrimination and for the rights of Dalits.

back.text: Srinivasa Ramanujan — Indian mathematician (1887–1920). Working largely from intuition, he made major contributions to number theory, infinite series, and continued fractions. His notebooks continue to inspire mathematical research.
back.markdown:
**Indian mathematician (1887–1920).**

{#0F766E}Why they matter{/}

- Working largely from intuition, he made major contributions to number theory, infinite series, and continued fractions.
- His notebooks continue to inspire mathematical research.

back.text: Sushruta — Ancient Indian physician traditionally dated to around the first millennium BCE. The Sushruta Samhita describes surgery, anatomy, and medical training in remarkable detail. His exact dates and the text's development remain debated.
back.markdown:
**Ancient Indian physician traditionally dated to around the first millennium BCE.**

{#0F766E}Why they matter{/}

- The Sushruta Samhita describes surgery, anatomy, and medical training in remarkable detail.
- His exact dates and the text's development remain debated.

back.text: José Martí — Cuban writer and independence activist (1853–1895). His essays and organizing helped inspire Cuba's struggle for independence from Spain. He became a foundational figure in Cuban national identity.
back.markdown:
**Cuban writer and independence activist (1853–1895).**

{#0F766E}Why they matter{/}

- His essays and organizing helped inspire Cuba's struggle for independence from Spain.
- He became a foundational figure in Cuban national identity.

front.markdown: Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz

back.text: Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz — Mexican writer, scholar, and nun of New Spain (c. 1648–1695). Her poetry and prose displayed exceptional learning and literary skill. She defended women's intellectual ability and access to education.
back.markdown:
**Mexican writer, scholar, and nun of New Spain (c. 1648–1695).**

{#0F766E}Why they matter{/}

- Her poetry and prose displayed exceptional learning and literary skill.
- She defended women's intellectual ability and access to education.

back.text: Gabriela Mistral — Chilean poet, educator, and diplomat (1889–1957). She became the first Latin American awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature. Her writing often explored love, grief, childhood, and social justice.
back.markdown:
**Chilean poet, educator, and diplomat (1889–1957).**

{#0F766E}Why they matter{/}

- She became the first Latin American awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature.
- Her writing often explored love, grief, childhood, and social justice.

back.text: Pachacuti — Inca ruler of the 15th century. He transformed the Kingdom of Cusco into the expanding Inca Empire. Tradition credits his reign with major administrative and building projects, though details rely partly on later accounts.
back.markdown:
**Inca ruler of the 15th century.**

{#0F766E}Why they matter{/}

- He transformed the Kingdom of Cusco into the expanding Inca Empire.
- Tradition credits his reign with major administrative and building projects, though details rely partly on later accounts.

back.text: Kamehameha I — Founder and first ruler of the unified Kingdom of Hawaiʻi (c. 1758–1819). He united most of the Hawaiian Islands through warfare and diplomacy. His government helped preserve Hawaiian independence during a period of growing foreign contact.
back.markdown:
**Founder and first ruler of the unified Kingdom of Hawaiʻi (c. 1758–1819).**

{#0F766E}Why they matter{/}

- He united most of the Hawaiian Islands through warfare and diplomacy.
- His government helped preserve Hawaiian independence during a period of growing foreign contact.

back.text: Queen Liliʻuokalani — Last sovereign monarch of the Hawaiian Kingdom (1838–1917). She resisted efforts to weaken Hawaiian sovereignty. She was overthrown in 1893 by a group supported by US diplomatic and military representatives.
back.markdown:
**Last sovereign monarch of the Hawaiian Kingdom (1838–1917).**

{#0F766E}Why they matter{/}

- She resisted efforts to weaken Hawaiian sovereignty.
- She was overthrown in 1893 by a group supported by US diplomatic and military representatives.

back.text: Te Rauparaha — Māori rangatira and military leader of Ngāti Toa (c. 1768–1849). He led major migrations and established Ngāti Toa power around the lower North Island and upper South Island. The haka “Ka Mate” is traditionally attributed to him.
back.markdown:
**Māori rangatira and military leader of Ngāti Toa (c. 1768–1849).**

{#0F766E}Why they matter{/}

- He led major migrations and established Ngāti Toa power around the lower North Island and upper South Island.
- The haka “Ka Mate” is traditionally attributed to him.

back.text: Kate Sheppard — New Zealand suffrage leader (1848–1934). She organized petitions and campaigning that helped New Zealand become the first self-governing country where women won national voting rights in 1893.

Āpirana Ngata — Māori politician, lawyer, and cultural leader (1874–1950). He promoted Māori land development, education, language, and arts. He was the first Māori graduate of a New Zealand university.
back.markdown:
**Māori politician, lawyer, and cultural leader (1874–1950).**

back.text: Dame Whina Cooper — Māori community leader and activist (1895–1994). At age 79 she led the 1975 Māori Land March across New Zealand. The march drew national attention to the continuing loss of Māori land.
back.markdown:
**Māori community leader and activist (1895–1994).**

{#0F766E}Why they matter{/}

- The march drew national attention to the continuing loss of Māori land.

back.text: Eddie Mabo — Meriam land-rights campaigner from the Torres Strait (1936–1992). The legal case bearing his name overturned the doctrine of terra nullius in Australian law. The decision recognized that Indigenous land rights could survive British colonization.
back.markdown:
**Meriam land-rights campaigner from the Torres Strait (1936–1992).**

{#0F766E}Why they matter{/}

- The decision recognized that Indigenous land rights could survive British colonization.

back.text: Albert Namatjira — Arrernte painter from Central Australia (1902–1959). His distinctive watercolours brought Aboriginal Australian landscapes to a wide national audience. His life also exposed discriminatory restrictions placed on Indigenous Australians.
back.markdown:
**Arrernte painter from Central Australia (1902–1959).**

back.text: Ratu Sir Lala Sukuna — Fijian chief, soldier, and statesman (1888–1958). He helped shape modern systems of Indigenous Fijian land administration. His public service strongly influenced Fiji's political development before independence.
back.markdown:
**Fijian chief, soldier, and statesman (1888–1958).**

back.text: Timur — Turco-Mongol conqueror and founder of the Timurid Empire (1336–1405). He built a vast empire centred on Samarkand through destructive military campaigns. Timurid patronage later supported major achievements in art, architecture, and scholarship.
back.markdown:
**Turco-Mongol conqueror and founder of the Timurid Empire (1336–1405).**

back.text: Babur — Central Asian prince and founder of the Mughal Empire (1483–1530). He conquered northern India after victory at Panipat in 1526. His memoir, the Baburnama, is an important record of his life and world.
back.markdown:
**Central Asian prince and founder of the Mughal Empire (1483–1530).**

back.text: Ulugh Beg — Timurid ruler and astronomer in Samarkand (1394–1449). He built a major observatory and sponsored precise observations of the stars. His astronomical tables were among the finest produced before telescopes.
back.markdown:
**Timurid ruler and astronomer in Samarkand (1394–1449).**

back.text: Al-Farabi — Philosopher and scholar from Central Asia (c. 870–950). He wrote influential works on logic, political philosophy, music, and metaphysics. Later thinkers called him the “Second Teacher” after Aristotle.
back.markdown:
**Philosopher and scholar from Central Asia (c. 870–950).**

back.text: Abai Qunanbaiuly — Kazakh poet, thinker, and cultural reformer (1845–1904). His poetry and prose encouraged education and intellectual renewal. He became a foundational figure in modern Kazakh literature.
back.markdown:

back.text: Tomyris — Queen associated with the Massagetae of Central Asia in the 6th century BCE. Herodotus says she defeated and killed Cyrus the Great in battle. Because the story comes from later Greek tradition, its details remain uncertain.

back.text: Ahmad Shah Durrani — Founder of the Durrani Empire in Afghanistan (c. 1722–1772). He united Afghan tribes and built an empire spanning parts of Central and South Asia. He is often regarded as a founder of the modern Afghan state.
